Amelia Earhart. The pioneering aviator who set numerous women's aviation records in the 1920s and 1930s and then vanished over the Pacific. In 1932, nearly five years after Charles Lindbergh crossed the Atlantic, Earhart became the first woman to fly solo across the ocean. Throughout the 1930s, she set women's altitude records, speed records, and cross-country distance records, consistently breaking barriers in an industry dominated by men. In 1937, she and navigator Fred Noonan departed on an attempt to circumnavigate the globe in a twin-engine Lockheed Electra. On July 2nd of that year, over the Pacific near Howland Island, she disappeared. Her final radio transmission indicated she was searching for Howland Island but couldn't find it. The cause of her disappearance remains officially unknown. She was just 39 years old. Earhart pioneered women's entry into aviation and challenged gender stereotypes through her writing and lectures, proving that women belonged in the cockpit. Her mysterious fate has captured the world's imagination for decades, spawning endless speculation and search efforts. She shares a father with Charles Lindbergh, who pioneered the transatlantic route five years before she did.
